Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

PARIS, France (CNN) -- Three French journalists charged in an alleged plot to kidnap African children for adoption in Europe arrived in Paris on Sunday, hours after French President Nicolas Sarkozy held emergency talks in Chad. But 14 other people remained in custody in the African nation, some facing serious charges that could send them to jail for up to 20 years. The journalists were among seven Europeans a Chadian judge released Sunday, including a Spanish flight crew, whom Sarkozy dropped off in a brief stop in Madrid on his way back from Chad. All were arrested last week after workers from Zoe's Ark -- a French-based charity group -- were accused of trying to fly 103 children out of Chad in a kidnapping and adoption operation.  Watch a report on how the events unfolded » . Some of the children may never return to their families because it is too difficult to determine their backgrounds, Red Cross spokeswoman Inah Kaloga told CNN on Friday. Those who remain under arrest in Chad are six members of the French charity, four Chadians and four remaining members of the flight crew. Some face kidnapping and fraud charges. Zoe's Ark leader Eric Breteau testified Saturday to a court in the Chadian capital that the three journalists and the flight crew of seven Spaniards and a Belgian were not involved in the alleged plot, court witnesses told CNN. At least some of the flight crew are scheduled to testify before a judge on Monday. The three journalists initially had been charged with complicity in the alleged kidnapping attempt. It's not clear if the charges against them have been dropped.  Watch the freed Europeans leave Chad » . In a joint news conference with Spanish Prime Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero on Sunday at Madrid's Torrejon Air Force Base, Sarkozy expressed satisfaction that some of those detained had been released. At the same time, however, he told reporters, "We should respect the sovereignty of Chad." Zapatero thanked Sarkozy for dropping the four Spanish flight crew members off in their home country, and thanked Chadian President Idriss Deby for allowing them to return. After his emergency talks in Chad, Sarkozy stressed the scandal would not affect the strong relations between the two countries or affect the planned deployment of a European force to protect refugees from Sudan's Darfur region who have fled to Chad and the neighboring Central African Republic. Sarkozy also said he hoped the six remaining French nationals -- all from Zoe's Ark -- would face trial in France. The charity says that the children were orphans from the Darfur region -- where the United Nations estimates 200,000 people have been killed in four years of conflict -- and that the group was taking them to host families in France. But after preliminary interviews with the children, aid agencies said Thursday it appeared most of them probably are not orphans and not from Sudan, but instead come from villages on the Chadian side of the border with Sudan. The children are staying in an Abeche orphanage while aid agencies and government officials try to find out where they came from -- a challenge hindered by the number of children, their youth, and the volatile situation in the region. A father of three of the children allegedly kidnapped told a French newspaper he put his children into the charity's care after he was told they would be educated at a school under construction in a nearby town. The Chadian man, who gave his name as Arbab, told Le Parisien on Sunday that workers from Zoe's Ark had visited his village three times. "They never said they would take away our children," he told the newspaper. E-mail to a friend . CNN's Nic Robertson and Al Goodman contributed to this report.

PARIS, France (CNN) — Three French reporters accused of involvement in a suspected scheme to abduct African children and place them with adoptive families in Europe returned to Paris on Sunday. Their arrival came only hours after French President Nicolas Sarkozy traveled to Chad for urgent discussions.

Fourteen other people were still being detained in Chad, however. Some faced serious criminal accusations carrying possible prison sentences of as long as 20 years.

A Chadian judge ordered the release of the journalists and four members of a Spanish flight crew on Sunday. On his return journey from Chad, Sarkozy made a short stop in Madrid to bring the Spanish crew members home.

The arrests took place the previous week after employees of Zoe’s Ark, a charity headquartered in France, were accused of attempting to fly 103 children out of Chad as part of an alleged abduction and adoption operation. A report explains how the case developed.

Red Cross spokeswoman Inah Kaloga told CNN on Friday that some of the children might never be reunited with their relatives because establishing their origins could prove too difficult.

Those still detained in Chad included six Zoe’s Ark workers, four Chadian nationals and four other members of the flight crew. Several were accused of kidnapping and fraud.

According to witnesses in the courtroom, Zoe’s Ark director Eric Breteau told a court in N’Djamena, the Chadian capital, on Saturday that neither the three journalists nor the flight crew—seven Spaniards and one Belgian—had participated in the alleged plan. At least some crew members were expected to appear before a judge on Monday.

The reporters were initially charged with assisting the alleged kidnapping attempt, but it remained uncertain whether those charges had been dismissed. Video showed the released Europeans departing Chad.

Speaking alongside Spanish Prime Minister Jose Luis Rodriguez Zapatero at Madrid’s Torrejon Air Force Base on Sunday, Sarkozy said he was pleased that several detainees had been freed. He also emphasized to journalists that Chad’s sovereignty had to be respected.

Zapatero expressed gratitude to Sarkozy for returning the four Spanish crew members to Spain. He also thanked Chadian President Idriss Deby for authorizing their release.

Following the emergency meeting in Chad, Sarkozy said the controversy would neither damage the close relationship between France and Chad nor disrupt the proposed deployment of European troops. That force was intended to protect refugees who had escaped violence in Sudan’s Darfur region and fled into Chad and the neighboring Central African Republic.

Sarkozy added that he wanted the six French citizens still in custody—all members of Zoe’s Ark—to be tried in France.

The charity maintained that the children were Darfur orphans whom it planned to place with host families in France. The United Nations estimated that 200,000 people had died during four years of conflict in Darfur.

Aid organizations said Thursday, however, that initial conversations with the children suggested most were probably neither orphans nor Sudanese. Instead, they appeared to be from villages in Chad near the Sudanese border.

The children were being housed at an orphanage in Abeche while humanitarian groups and government authorities worked to identify their places of origin. The investigation was complicated by the children’s large number, their young ages and the region’s instability.

A man who said three of his children were among those allegedly abducted told a French newspaper that he had entrusted them to the organization after being informed they would attend a school being built in a nearby town.

The Chadian father, who identified himself as Arbab, told *Le Parisien* on Sunday that Zoe’s Ark representatives had come to his village on three occasions. He said they had never told villagers that the children would be taken away.

The original report included an option to email the story to a friend. CNN correspondents Nic Robertson and Al Goodman also contributed.

counterfactuals.output:
# A rescue mission unraveled: Inside the 2007 Zoe’s Ark controversy

**N’DJAMENA, Chad —** It was presented as an emergency humanitarian evacuation: More than 100 children, described by a French charity as orphans fleeing the war in Sudan’s Darfur region, would be flown from Chad to new lives with families in France.

Instead, the October 2007 operation ended on an airport tarmac in eastern Chad, with children taken off a chartered aircraft and European aid workers, journalists and flight crew placed under arrest.

The case became an international crisis almost overnight. Chadian authorities accused members of the French group Zoe’s Ark of trying to abduct 103 children. French President Nicolas Sarkozy made an urgent trip to Chad to negotiate the release of several Europeans, while humanitarian agencies began investigating a question at the center of the scandal: Were the children really Darfur orphans at all?

Evidence gathered in the following days suggested that most were neither from Darfur nor orphans.

## The operation at Abéché

Zoe’s Ark, operating in Chad under the name **Children Rescue**, had told prospective French host families that it planned to evacuate children endangered by the conflict in Darfur.

The war in western Sudan had displaced millions of people and sent refugees across the border into eastern Chad. Against that backdrop, the charity argued that the children faced grave danger and needed urgent protection.

On October 25, 2007, Chadian authorities stopped the group at the airport in Abéché, a major humanitarian hub near the Sudanese border. The 103 children were about to be placed aboard a chartered aircraft bound for Europe.

Officials said the group did not have authorization to remove the children from Chad or complete the international adoption procedures that would have been required.

The circumstances immediately raised alarm. Some of the children had been wrapped in bandages, and witnesses and investigators alleged they had been made to look injured to support the account that they were victims of the Darfur war. Members of the charity denied that they were engaged in child trafficking and insisted they believed they were carrying out a humanitarian rescue.

Chadian President Idriss Déby publicly denounced the operation, suggesting the children might have been intended for adoption, exploitation or even organ trafficking. No evidence emerged to substantiate the most extreme allegations, but his statements reflected the anger the case generated in Chad.

## Kidnapping and fraud charges

Chadian prosecutors brought serious criminal accusations against the six principal French members of Zoe’s Ark.

They were charged with offenses including the **abduction of minors** and **fraud**. Members of the Spanish flight crew and a Belgian pilot were initially accused of complicity, although the extent of their knowledge about the operation was disputed. Three French journalists who had accompanied the group were also detained but maintained they were there to report on the mission, not to participate in it.

The French charity workers argued that they had acted in good faith. They said intermediaries and local contacts had led them to believe the children were Sudanese refugees who had lost their parents.

Chadian authorities rejected that explanation, saying the group had bypassed national law and attempted to take children out of the country under false pretenses.

In December 2007, a Chadian court convicted the six Zoe’s Ark workers of kidnapping children and sentenced them to **eight years of forced labor**. Under a judicial cooperation agreement, they were later transferred to France, where the sentence was converted into an eight-year prison term. Déby pardoned them in March 2008, and they were released.

## Sarkozy’s emergency trip

The arrests created immediate pressure on Sarkozy’s government. The case involved French citizens, strained relations with a strategically important African country and risked overshadowing France’s broader role in responding to the crises in Chad and Darfur.

On November 4, 2007, Sarkozy flew to N’Djamena for emergency talks with Déby.

After the meeting, Sarkozy left Chad with **seven of the detained Europeans**: the **three French journalists** and **four Spanish flight attendants**. The presidential aircraft stopped in Madrid before continuing to France.

Sarkozy portrayed the trip as an effort to secure the release of people who appeared not to have played a central role in organizing the operation. But the high-profile intervention prompted criticism.

Some French legal experts and opposition figures questioned whether a president should personally intervene in an active criminal case abroad. In Chad, critics said the episode showed how quickly European governments could exert pressure when their own citizens were detained, even as Chadian authorities insisted their courts should be allowed to proceed independently.

The remaining Spanish crew members and the Belgian pilot were released later after investigators concluded they had not been fully aware of the charity’s plan. The six core Zoe’s Ark members remained in custody and went to trial.

## Were the children from Darfur?

The identities and family circumstances of the 103 children became one of the most damaging aspects of the case.

Zoe’s Ark had presented them as orphans from Darfur, the region whose humanitarian catastrophe had drawn worldwide attention. But interviews conducted by the United Nations refugee agency, UNICEF, the International Committee of the Red Cross and other organizations produced a very different picture.

Investigators found that **most of the children were Chadian**, not Sudanese. Many came from villages near the border, and a large majority said they had at least one living parent or another close family member.

Humanitarian agencies reported that dozens of parents had entrusted their children to local intermediaries after being told the children would receive schooling or care — not that they would be flown permanently to Europe.

The children’s backgrounds varied, and eastern Chad itself had suffered from violence, displacement and poverty. Some may have been living in precarious conditions. But humanitarian officials emphasized that poverty or insecurity did not make a child an orphan, nor did it permit removal from the country without family consent and legal safeguards.

The findings undercut the charity’s central justification for the flight.

## Families in France were waiting

Before the arrests, hundreds of families in France had reportedly expressed interest in receiving children through Zoe’s Ark. Some had paid money to the organization and believed they were participating in an emergency foster-care program rather than a conventional adoption.

French authorities had warned the charity that any transfer of children would have to comply with international law and Chad’s domestic procedures. The French Foreign Ministry had also raised concerns about the project before the attempted airlift.

The controversy exposed the risks of so-called emergency adoption during war and disaster. Child-protection specialists say that in chaotic conditions, children can easily be misidentified as orphans when they have surviving parents who are temporarily separated from them.

International standards generally prioritize tracing relatives and reuniting families. Moving children across borders is supposed to be a last resort, carried out only after their identities and legal status have been carefully established.

## A case that damaged humanitarian trust

The Zoe’s Ark affair reverberated beyond the defendants and the children.

Aid organizations working in eastern Chad feared the scandal would make local communities suspicious of legitimate humanitarian programs. Many agencies had spent years building trust with refugees and Chadian families, and the attempted airlift fueled fears that foreigners might remove children under the guise of assistance.

The case also prompted broader questions about a model of humanitarian activism driven by urgency and moral certainty but lacking professional oversight.

Zoe’s Ark portrayed itself as acting where governments and major aid agencies had failed. Critics said that conviction led the group to ignore warnings, legal requirements and basic child-protection standards.

For the 103 children, the story did not end with the airport arrests. Humanitarian groups worked to identify them, trace their relatives and return many of them to their communities.

The scandal’s central claim — that an airplane full of Darfur orphans was being rescued from war — proved deeply misleading. What authorities found instead was a group of mostly Chadian children, many with living families, caught in an unauthorized operation that transformed a purported act of compassion into a diplomatic and criminal crisis.
